title: USB device not detected
summary: Covers the whole path from cable and port through to drivers and dying hardware, tested in the order that costs least.

which_device.question: What kind of USB device is not detected?
which_device.help: Storage devices behave differently from peripherals, and USB-C docking stations have their own common failure.

options.label: USB drive, external hard drive or card reader
Keyboard, mouse or other peripheral
Phone or tablet
A dock, hub or multi-port adapter
A USB-C device such as a charger, webcam or headset

storage_device_test.question: Does the drive appear in File Explorer, or is it missing entirely?
storage_device_test.help: Check This PC under This PC and also Disk Management, since a drive can be present but not assigned a letter.

options.label: It does not appear anywhere
It appears in Disk Management but not File Explorer
It appears but shows raw or unallocated space
It appears with a warning icon or asks to be formatted

no_drive_letter.question: Can you assign a drive letter in Disk Management?
no_drive_letter.help: Right-click the volume in Disk Management and choose Change Drive Letter and Paths. This is data-safe and reversible.

options.label: Yes, it works after assigning a letter
No, Disk Management reports an error
Disk Management does not show the disk at all

port_and_cable.question: Have you tried a different USB port and a different cable?
port_and_cable.help: USB ports on the front of a case and hubs are weaker. Cables that only carry power or data, not both, are common.

options.label: No, same port and cable
Yes, tried another port and cable

device_manager_check.question: Does the device appear in Device Manager, and does it show a yellow exclamation mark?
device_manager_check.help: Press Win plus X and choose Device Manager, then look for Unknown USB Device, which usually means a driver is missing.

options.label: It shows Unknown USB Device or a yellow exclamation mark
It is greyed out
It does not appear at all
It appears and looks normal

phone_connection.question: Have you tried the cable the phone came with, and a different USB port?
phone_connection.help: Many cheap USB-C cables are power-only and never transfer data. A phone also needs a mode selected on screen.

options.label: No, using a spare cable
Yes, used the original cable
Yes, but nothing happens at all

phone_mode.question: Does the phone show a notification offering file transfer, charging only, or USB debugging?
phone_mode.help: The notification appears on the phone, not the PC, and must be tapped to allow data transfer.

options.label: Yes, and I chose file transfer
It only offers charging
No notification appears on the phone

dock_power.question: Is the dock connected to a power adapter as well as the PC?
dock_power.help: Most docks need their own power supply. Bus-powered devices without one simply will not be detected.

options.label: Yes, power adapter connected
No, it is plug-and-play only
I do not know

dock_port_check.question: Is the dock plugged into a rear motherboard port rather than a front panel or hub port?
dock_port_check.help: Docks are demanding devices and need the full bandwidth a rear port provides.

options.label: Yes, rear port
No, front panel or through a hub

usb_c_device.question: Does the USB-C port deliver any sign of life: charging, a light, or any sound?
usb_c_device.help: This tells you whether the port itself works at all, separately from data.

options.label: It charges but data does not work
Nothing at all happens
It works sometimes and stops

usb_c_clean.question: Have you inspected and cleaned the USB-C port?
usb_c_clean.help: Pocket lint is the single most common cause of a USB-C port that only works at certain angles.

options.label: No, I have not looked at it
Yes, it is clean and still intermittent
It is clean and completely dead

result_cable_and_port.title: Try a different cable and port
result_cable_and_port.diagnosis: Cables and ports fail far more often than the devices themselves, and swapping both costs nothing.
steps: Test with a different known-good USB cable; cheap cables often lack data lines entirely
Move to a rear motherboard port, which has more power and bandwidth than a front panel port
Avoid hubs and extension cables for the first test, since they add a failure point
On a laptop, try both sides, since ports differ in power delivery on some models
For USB-C, check the port with a torch for lint and clear it gently with a wooden toothpick
Check the cable length: cables over 3 metres often fail on high-speed transfers
warnings: Do not use metal tools or tweezers inside a USB port; you can short the contacts and permanently damage the port.
Yank cables out of sockets rather than unplugging them; the solder joints at the device end fail first.

result_usb_driver.title: Install the right USB driver
result_usb_driver.diagnosis: Unknown USB Device means Windows found hardware it has no driver for, which is normal and easy to fix.
steps: Open Device Manager and expand Universal Serial Bus controllers
Also check Portable Devices and any entry named Unknown USB Device
Right-click the unknown device and choose Update driver
Choose Search automatically for drivers, and let Windows try its built-in catalogue first
If that fails, download the driver from your PC vendor's support page for your exact model
For USB storage, update the chipset driver as well, since it manages USB power management
After installing, run Scan for hardware changes from the Action menu
warnings: Do not use driver updater tools or third-party driver packs. They install unsigned drivers that Windows may refuse to load.
Avoid the optional Windows Update driver for USB hardware unless the vendor one is unavailable; version mismatches cause intermittent failures.

result_enable_usb.title: Enable the device
result_enable_usb.diagnosis: A greyed-out entry is disabled, which is a setting rather than a fault.
steps: Right-click the greyed-out device and choose Enable device
If that option is missing, uninstall the device and restart, then let Windows reinstall it
Check View > Show hidden devices, since disabled devices appear greyed out there
Run Scan for hardware changes from the Action menu after enabling
Restart Windows so the driver loads at startup
Check whether a USB port is disabled in BIOS, since some boards can disable individual ports

result_usb_hardware.title: The port or device has failed
result_usb_hardware.diagnosis: When the device does not appear anywhere and other devices work in the same port, the hardware is at fault.
steps: Test the suspect port with a different device to confirm the port works
Test the suspect device in a different port or on another computer
If it fails everywhere, the device has failed and needs replacing
For a desktop, check whether the front-panel USB header or case buttons are wired to the wrong header on the motherboard
On a laptop, inspect the port for bent pins or lint with a torch
Update the chipset driver, which can restore badly behaved ports even when the device is listed
warnings: Do not force a connector that does not seat easily. Damaged ports usually cannot be repaired except by board-level work.
A failed USB device can be drawing excessive current. Stop using it if you notice a warm port or any smell of burning.

result_drive_letter.title: Assign the drive a letter
result_drive_letter.diagnosis: The drive is detected but has no letter, so File Explorer cannot show it. This is data-safe.
steps: Open Disk Management: right-click Start > Disk Management
Find the drive by its size and format
Right-click its volume and choose Change Drive Letter and Paths
Choose Add and assign an unused letter such as F:
If it reports that the partition is RAW or unformatted, do not format it, since that will erase the data
Use our disk health script to check the drive's SMART data before doing anything else to it
warnings: Never format a drive that contains data you have not backed up. Formatting is not a reliable way to repair a drive and destroys whatever is still recoverable.
A drive appearing as RAW usually means the filesystem is damaged or the drive is failing.

result_drive_recovery.title: Recover the drive's data first
result_drive_recovery.diagnosis: Windows asking to format a drive means it cannot read the filesystem. That is a data situation, not a formatting one.
steps: Stop using the drive immediately and do not format it, because formatting can destroy recoverable data
Check the drive's SMART health using our disk health script; a failing drive needs data recovered, not repaired
If the drive is clicky, slow or drops off the system, replace it rather than attempting repairs
Try a data recovery tool such as TestDisk or PhotoRec, which work on raw devices without writing to the drive
Check for another copy: OneDrive, File History, a backup, or the same folder on another machine
If the drive is failing, professional recovery is the only safe option, since further use reduces the chance of recovery
warnings: Do not run chkdsk with /f on a drive with unrecoverable data. It writes to the drive and can destroy what is left.
Do not keep re-plugging a failing drive, since each attempt stresses it further.
If the drive contains work or photos with no backup, stop and seek professional data recovery before experimenting.

result_dock_power.title: Power the dock properly
result_dock_power.diagnosis: A dock without its power supply often shows nothing at all, or only works with a few devices attached.
steps: Connect the dock's power adapter, which most docks require even when connected to mains
Plug the host cable into a rear motherboard port rather than a front panel port or a hub
Reduce the number of attached devices and test one at a time to find the failing one
Remove external monitors first, since two displays can exceed the dock's display output capability
Check the dock's firmware or driver software from its manufacturer
Confirm your PC's USB port supports the dock's connection, since USB 2.0 cannot drive two displays
warnings: Do not power a bus-powered dock from a laptop while also charging the laptop from the same dock. This can cause power problems in both devices.
Use only the power supply supplied with the dock, since mismatched supplies can damage it.

result_phone_transfer.title: Set the phone to file transfer mode
result_phone_transfer.diagnosis: Android phones default to charging-only over USB, so the PC sees no storage at all until you change it.
steps: Connect the phone and unlock it; the notification only appears on a locked-screen-capable connection
Pull down the notification shade and tap the USB notification
Choose File transfer or Android Auto, not Just charging
If no notification appears, tap the USB icon in Settings > Connected devices > USB preferences and select File transfer
Enable USB debugging in Developer options only if a specific tool requires it, and disable it afterwards
Try the original cable, since many third-party USB-C cables are power-only
warnings: Turn USB debugging off after use. Leaving debugging enabled allows any computer with your authorisation to control your phone.
Do not enable 'Charge only' with 'Allow access to all files' permanently on an untrusted computer.

result_usb_power.title: Check power delivery
result_usb_power.diagnosis: A device that appears correctly but will not run is usually being starved of power, especially when connected through a hub.
steps: Move the device from any hub or extension cable to a port directly on the PC
If the device has its own power adapter, connect it before testing
Check whether the device is drawing more than one port can supply, which affects an entire bus of devices
Try the port directly beside it, since some adjacent pairs share one controller
Update the chipset driver, since it manages USB power management
On a desktop, check whether any other devices are drawing excess current and disabling the same controller
warnings: Do not leave a device connected if the port becomes unusually warm, since that indicates overload.
Always use the power adapter supplied with the device rather than drawing power from the PC where possible.

result_usb_c_port.title: Clean the USB-C port
result_usb_c_port.diagnosis: Pocket lint is the most common cause of a USB-C port that only charges at certain angles.
steps: Power off and unplug the device before inspecting the port
Look into the port with a torch to see compacted lint at the back
Clear it gently with a wooden toothpick or a plastic SIM card tray tool, using the flat side
Work from the edges inward and never force anything metal into the port
Blow out loose debris with compressed air if available
Test again; if it still fails, the port's contacts are worn and need solder-level repair
warnings: Never use metal tweezers, a knife, or a paperclip in a USB-C port. This bends or shorts the internal contacts and can destroy the port.
Do not power the device while cleaning the port.
If the port is bent or has a wobbly tongue, stop using it and get it repaired, since further use can damage the board.
